body:
The account diagnoses well, but several of its parts do not sit well with each other, and in places it treats as cheap what is not cheap.

First, an internal tension. The third conjecture says the friend avoids the conversations because of what they cost him, yet the remedy prescribes more structured conversation: a process conversation, a recurring check-in, pre-negotiated remedy talks, plus the separate talk. If the irritant is conversational cost, the program schedules the irritant weekly — time-boxed this time, but recurring and hard to skip. Relatedly, the account iterates on a single allocation mechanism — per-instance negotiated assignment — and never considers the standard alternative of standing domain ownership, where each person owns an area end-to-end, timing is at the owner's discretion, and almost no recurring negotiation is needed at all. The problem text itself is evidence that per-instance negotiation is the failing component; the choice to optimize that mechanism rather than replace it is made without argument, and it is the choice that maximizes dependence on the friend who avoids talking.

Second, the memory conjecture has a rival the account never engages. "Memory fills the gaps differently for each of you" presumes symmetric, honest reconstruction. But reinterpretation disputes in shared flats are often driven by asymmetric tolerance for mess and motivated reading: both parties remember, each reads the agreement toward less work, or one party minds less and waits for the others to fold. Under that rival, writing it down does not end the disputes, it relocates them — to the meaning of the written words and to who holds the burden where the wording runs out. The account's own fallback, explicit done-criteria, assumes chore language can be made exhaustive; it cannot. The proposed test (two to four weeks of written agreements ending the disputes) conflates the two hypotheses, because motivated interpretation predicts persistence with disputes now attached to the text itself.

Third, the tests are weaker than they look. The check-in attendance test is confounded by the account's own second conjecture: if schedules genuinely churn, recurring absence from a fixed meeting is expected for reasons unrelated to the procedural reading, so absenteeism cannot cleanly indict it. And the remedy menu — swaps, trades, the shared pot — presumes the ongoing participation of the member the diagnosis identifies as least likely to participate. The hardest realistic case is not refusal to attend but assent followed by non-performance: agreements get written and then ignored. Nothing in the account binds that case.

Fourth, sequencing and cost. On the account's own epistemics, the cheapest and most diagnostic step — the low-stakes separate talk — should come first, since its outcome decides which of the three conjectures even applies; instead it is fifth, after steps that assume the conjectures hold. The concession in the commitments that the narrator's own contribution is invisible cuts deeper than the account allows: combined with the avoidance-as-cost conjecture, it leaves open that part of the cost the friend avoids is the narrator, and convening process reform before probing that builds on sand. Finally, "almost no cost" does not survive inspection: someone must administer the log, convene the check-in, and enforce the remedies, and that someone will be the narrator — a managerial role apt to generate exactly the role-resentment the system is meant to dissolve, with the added risk that a written ledger among friends reads as assembling a case file.

My objection could itself be mistaken. Ownership allocation also needs an initial negotiation the avoider may refuse, so it inherits the bootstrapping problem rather than escaping it; and if the disputes really are only about ambiguity, the written-log fix may be exactly right and my alternatives beside the point.
commitments: Taking up this objection means treating four criticisms as live but unproven. (1) The claimed tension between a conversation-cost diagnosis and a conversation-heavy remedy commits me to the existence and feasibility of lower-conversation architectures such as standing domain ownership; it loses force if per-instance negotiation is failing only at the level of wording rather than as a mechanism, and I concede the ownership alternative inherits the account's own bootstrapping problem since it too requires an initial negotiation the avoider may refuse. (2) The motivated-interpretation and asymmetric-tolerance rival is a conjecture resting on facts not exposed in the problem text; a cheap discriminator is available — disputes over the meaning of specific written items support the rival, while disputes about whether anything was agreed support the memory conjecture — and my sequencing criticism, if applied by moving the separate low-stakes talk first, would itself produce evidence for or against the rival. (3) The confounding criticism of the attendance test commits me to claiming the account's tests are weakly identifying until schedule constraints are ruled out, not to claiming its conjectures are false. (4) The sequencing and administration-cost claims depend on the narrator's actual role in the flat dynamic and on who would run the proposed system; these cannot be verified from the exposed material, so adopting them means asking rather than asserting. Criticisms I accept in advance: the account already hedges its program and disclaims adjudicating current disputes, so part of my pressure lands on language it qualified; my strategic-behavior framing may overweight calculation against temperament, fatigue, or low mood as causes of avoidance; and nothing here settles whether an alternative architecture fits the flat's money constraints or standards gap, or which flatmate, if any, is in the right.
